clinicalPearls: Factor I is the serine protease that inactivates C3b and C4b; complete deficiency removes a key brake on the alternative complement pathway
Uncontrolled C3 consumption produces a persistently low C3 with a normal C4 and characteristic secondary reduction of factor B and factor H
The dominant clinical problem in complete deficiency is recurrent invasive infection with encapsulated organisms, especially meningococcal and pneumococcal disease, resembling primary C3 deficiency

Factor I is only active in the presence of cofactors (factor H and complement receptor 1 for C3b; C4b-binding protein and membrane cofactor protein/CD46 for C4b), so its deficiency phenotypically overlaps with factor H deficiency
Heterozygous CFI variants are recognised risk factors for atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and C3 glomerulopathy
Some patients show autoimmune or inflammatory features that reflect impaired clearance of immune complexes and complement activation products
Complete deficiency is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, so family screening and genetic counselling are appropriate
reference.pathophysiology: Factor I, encoded by CFI, is a plasma serine protease whose physiological role is the regulated proteolytic inactivation of the central complement opsonins C3b and C4b, acting only when the appropriate cofactor proteins are present (factor H and complement receptor 1 for C3b; C4b-binding protein and membrane cofactor protein for C4b). Loss of factor I activity removes the principal means of degrading C3b, so the alternative pathway amplification loop runs unchecked, continuously regenerating C3 convertase and consuming C3 and factor B; circulating C3 therefore falls while classical-pathway-dependent C4 remains normal, and factor H is consumed secondarily. The persistently depleted C3 impairs opsonisation and terminal pathway activity, leaving the host vulnerable to encapsulated bacteria in a pattern that mirrors C3 deficiency. When regulation is only partially impaired, the residual unchecked complement activity is expressed at vulnerable surfaces such as the glomerular endothelium, producing thrombotic microangiopathy or C3 glomerulopathy rather than the infection phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Factor H deficiency and other alternative pathway regulator defects (membrane cofactor protein/CD46)
Terminal complement component or properdin deficiency presenting with neisserial infection
Gain-of-function C3 or factor B variants driving complement consumption
Other causes of atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome or C3 glomerulopathy
Secondary hypocomplementaemia from immune complex disease or sepsis
additionalInvestigations: Complement screen demonstrating low C3 with normal C4
Factor I antigenic level and functional activity
Factor H and factor B levels, which are often secondarily reduced and help distinguish the pattern
CFI gene sequencing, with consideration of variants in cofactor genes
Alternative and total complement functional assays (AP50 and CH50)
Renal biopsy with complement staining if glomerulopathy or thrombotic microangiopathy is suspected
redFlags: Signs of invasive meningococcal or pneumococcal disease requiring emergency treatment
Recurrent or unusually severe bacterial meningitis or septicaemia
Acute kidney injury with microangiopathic haemolysis suggesting atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome
reference.prognosis: With immunisation against encapsulated organisms and prompt treatment of infection the outlook for complete deficiency is generally good, though a lifelong infection risk persists. The associated renal phenotypes (atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and C3 glomerulopathy) may progress to kidney failure but can respond to complement-directed therapy.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because a low C3 with normal C4 is not recognised as an alternative pathway regulator defect
Confusing the biochemical picture with factor H deficiency without measuring factor I directly
Assuming a normal antigenic factor I level excludes a functional defect
Neglecting encapsulated-organism vaccination and a standby antibiotic plan
Overlooking heterozygous carriers, who may still be at risk of complement-mediated kidney disease
management: Immunise against encapsulated organisms - meningococcal, pneumococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccines - as the mainstay of preventing invasive infection
Treat pyogenic and neisserial infections promptly with appropriate antibiotics and consider long-term antibiotic prophylaxis
Provide patients with an emergency plan and a low threshold for urgent assessment and empirical antibiotics in febrile illness
Treat associated atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome with a terminal complement C5 inhibitor and renal replacement therapy as required, with meningococcal cover before dosing
Manage C3 glomerulopathy and other renal involvement with complement-directed therapy and nephrology support
Provide genetic counselling and family screening given the autosomal recessive inheritance
